title: Slow Down and Look
description: How long people really look at art, and a simple method for looking longer and better

concepts.title: The 27-Second Glance
concepts.contentHtml:
Walk into any big museum and watch the people in front of the most famous paintings. The psychologists Jeffrey K. Smith and Lisa F. Smith did exactly that at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, timing visitors in front of great works for a study published in 2001. The average visitor looked for 27.2 seconds.1 The median was 17 seconds, and the most common time of all was just 10 seconds.

You might blame phones, but the numbers barely moved. Fifteen years later the Smiths and Pablo Tinio repeated the study at the Art Institute of Chicago, with more visitors, more kinds of artwork and separate timings for reading the labels. The mean was 28.63 seconds, the median 21 seconds and the mode, again, 10 seconds.2 Neither gender nor age made a significant difference. What had changed was how people spent those seconds: so many visitors took selfies with the paintings that the researchers coined a word for them, arties.

Ten seconds is enough to recognise a picture, but not to read it. Think of the difference between glancing at a page of text and reading it. A painting is a dense surface of decisions: where the figures stand, which colours sit next to each other, where the light falls, what each object might mean. Very little of that arrives in the first glance.

This topic is a toolkit for the rest of the looking. You will learn to see composition (how a picture steers your eye), colour and value (lightness and darkness), light, perspective and symbols, and then what conservators find beneath the paint and how a picture's setting changes what it says. The chemistry of the paint itself belongs to the sibling topic on pigments. Here the question is always the same: what is this picture doing to your eyes, and why?

concepts.title: Three Hours with a Flying Squirrel
concepts.contentHtml:
If ten seconds is normal, what happens at the other extreme? The Harvard art historian Jennifer Roberts gives every student in her courses the same deliberately excessive first task. Before reading anything about the work of art they have chosen, they must go and look at it for three full hours, writing down what they notice and the questions it raises. The time span is designed to seem too long, and students often resist: how can one small picture hold three hours of things to see?

Roberts did the exercise herself on A Boy with a Flying Squirrel, painted in Boston in 1765 by the young John Singleton Copley and now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. A boy, shown in profile, sits at a table holding a fine chain attached to a flying squirrel, with a glass of water beside his hand and a curtain behind him. Her notes show how slowly the picture gave itself up:

  • after 9 minutes, she saw that the shape of the boy's ear echoes the ruff of fur along the squirrel's belly;1
  • after 21 minutes, that the fingers holding the chain exactly span the diameter of the water glass beneath them;
  • after about 45 minutes, that the seemingly random folds of the curtain repeat the shapes of the boy's ear and eye.

Those details became central to her published interpretation. The glass of water is the only one Copley ever painted, and Roberts links it, and the profile pose familiar from coins, to the picture's own slow journey: Copley shipped it across the Atlantic to be judged by painters in London, and about 11 months passed before he learned their verdict, that his work was rather "too liney".

Her lesson is blunt: just because you have looked at something does not mean you have seen it.2 You will rarely have three hours. But ten deliberate minutes with a notebook will show you things that a 17-second visit never will.

concepts.title: Your Question Steers Your Eyes
concepts.contentHtml:
Looking is not a camera passively recording. The Russian scientist Alfred Yarbus (1914–86), whose book on eye movements reached English readers in 1967, recorded where people's eyes went as they examined Ilya Repin's They Did Not Expect Him (1884–88, oil on canvas, 160.5 by 167.5 cm, Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow). A political exile, clutching his hat, has walked unannounced into his family's sitting room. His mother rises from her armchair, his wife, at the piano, smiles uncertainly, a small girl at the table eyes him warily, and a maid still holds the door.

Yarbus asked the same person to view the painting seven times, each time with a different instruction:1 look freely; estimate how well off the family is; give the people's ages; guess what they were doing before the visitor arrived; remember their clothes; remember where people and objects are; estimate how long the visitor had been away. Each recording lasted 3 minutes. The pattern of eye movements changed dramatically with the question, because, as Yarbus put it, different information is found in different parts of a picture. Early in a viewing, the eyes went particularly to the faces.

The practical lesson: bring questions, and you will see more. Project Zero, a research centre at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, teaches a three-step routine called2 See, Think, Wonder:

  • See: describe exactly what is there, not what you assume. "A man in a long coat stands inside a doorway", not "a sad homecoming".
  • Think: say what you think is going on, and back it with evidence: what do you see that makes you say that?
  • Wonder: list the questions that remain. Who is he? Why does the girl look so wary?

Art historians use the same order (describe, then analyse, then interpret), and you will meet a famous version of it in the lesson on symbols. Keep to the order. Jumping straight to what a picture means is the commonest way to miss what is actually on the canvas.

title: Composition: Where the Eye Travels
description: Focal points, leading lines, balance, and the truth about the rule of thirds and the golden ratio

concepts.title: Focal Points and Leading Lines
concepts.contentHtml:
Composition is the arrangement of everything inside the frame. A good composition works like a route map: it tells your eye where to land first and how to travel from there. Painters steer you with a handful of reliable tools:

  • Contrast: the eye goes to the lightest light against the darkest dark, the most intense colour, the sharpest detail.
  • Faces and hands: as Yarbus found, viewers seek out faces early.
  • Leading lines: edges, limbs, gazes, roads and floorboards that run towards the main subject.
  • Isolation: a figure set apart by empty space.

Look at Caravaggio's Supper at Emmaus (1601, oil on canvas, 141 by 196.2 cm, National Gallery, London). At an inn table laid with bread, a roast bird and a basket of fruit, the risen Christ, young and beardless in a red tunic, blesses the bread, and two disciples suddenly recognise him. The National Gallery describes how the back of the disciple on the left and the outstretched arms of the one on the right, shown in extreme foreshortening, act like tram lines focusing attention on Christ's face.1 Christ and the disciples form an inward-facing triangle; the innkeeper stands outside it, his face in shadow.

Repin uses the floor in the same way in They Did Not Expect Him. He sets the mother's armchair and the table off centre, so the lines of the floorboards carry your eye straight to the returning exile.2

Linear perspective, which you will meet in lesson 5, is the most powerful leading-line machine of all. Every receding edge points to a single vanishing point, and because the eye travels to that point, Renaissance painters liked to put something important there. Next time you stand in front of a picture, trace the three or four strongest lines and see where they meet. Very often the painter is waiting for you there.

concepts.title: Balance and the Real Rule of Thirds
concepts.contentHtml:
A picture also has balance, a sense of how visual weight is spread across it. Large, dark, bright or busy shapes feel heavy; empty space feels light. Symmetrical balance, with matching halves around a central figure, feels stable and formal, which is why so many altarpieces use it. Asymmetrical balance sets a heavy mass against smaller or more distant ones, like an adult and a child on a seesaw, and feels more alive.

Imbalance can carry meaning. In Harmen Steenwyck's Still Life: An Allegory of the Vanities of Human Life (about 1640, oil on oak, 39.2 by 50.7 cm, National Gallery, London), books, a lute, a shell, a Japanese sword and a skull are heaped on a table below a diagonal running right across the panel. Above that diagonal is almost nothing, crossed only by a shaft of light along the opposite diagonal. Riches on one side, emptiness on the other: the lopsided design is the message.

Now the famous rule of thirds, which tells photographers to divide the frame with two horizontal and two vertical lines and put the subject where they cross. Here is a surprise. The phrase first appears in 1797, in a book on picturesque scenery by the English engraver John Thomas Smith, and it began as a rule about light and shade. Smith had noticed that in pictures by the best masters, especially Rembrandt, the main light is usually placed near the middle and more than two-thirds of the picture is in shadow. By analogy he suggested breaking lines and masses in a similar ratio: in a landscape, give the sky about two-thirds or about one-third, and in general prefer two-to-one over a formal half.

So painters before 1797 were not following a rule of thirds by name, and Smith's own version was about proportions of light, shadow, sky and land, not a grid. What he noticed is real enough: unequal divisions usually feel livelier than halves. Treat the thirds as one way of seeing that, not as a law.

concepts.title: The Golden Ratio Myth
concepts.contentHtml:
You have probably seen a famous painting with a golden spiral or rectangle drawn over it. The golden ratio, about 1.618 and written φ, is a genuinely remarkable number in mathematics, and books often claim that Leonardo and others built their paintings on it. The evidence is far weaker than the diagrams suggest.

Take the commonest claim, that a rectangle drawn around the face of the Mona Lisa has golden proportions. As the scientist and self-confessed art fanatic Mario Livio points out, there is no documentation that Leonardo consciously used the golden ratio in that painting, and nothing fixes where exactly the rectangle should be drawn.1 That is the deeper problem. A painting is full of edges, so if you measure enough lengths and divide them in enough ways, some ratio will land near 1.618 by chance. Livio warns that the literature is bursting with false claims about the ratio in art, naming Giotto, Seurat and Mondrian.

There is a fair point on the other side. Leonardo was a close friend of the mathematician Luca Pacioli, who published Divina Proportione, a treatise on the ratio, in 1509. And at least one painter certainly used it: the proportions of Salvador Dalí's Sacrament of the Last Supper equal the golden ratio, and a huge dodecahedron, a solid with twelve pentagonal faces, hangs over the table.

Do people simply prefer golden rectangles? In the 1860s the German physicist and psychologist Gustav Fechner showed people ten rectangles; 76% of choices fell on ratios of 1.75, 1.62 and 1.50, peaking at 1.62.2 Later work is mixed. Michael Godkewitsch concluded in 1974 that the preference was an artefact of where the golden rectangle sat in the range on offer. Chris McManus found moderately good evidence for Fechner's effect in 1980, but said it was very unclear whether the golden section itself mattered rather than similar ratios such as 1.5 or 1.75. The fair summary: people may like rectangles of roughly that shape, but a spiral drawn over a painting proves almost nothing.

title: Colour and Value
description: Hue, saturation and value, warm and cool, complementary contrast, and why value matters most

concepts.title: Hue, Saturation, Value
concepts.contentHtml:
Painters describe any colour by three properties. Hue is its family: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet. Saturation (also called chroma) is its intensity, from a pure, vivid red to a greyed, muted one. Value is how light or dark it is, from white to black. Two colours can share a hue and differ completely in value, like pale pink and deep maroon.

Painters also sort hues into warm (reds, oranges, yellows) and cool (blues, greens, many violets). The words are metaphors, but they shape how a picture feels and how it builds space. Leonardo's Virgin of the Rocks (painted between 1491 and 1508, oil on poplar, nearly 190 by 120 cm, National Gallery, London) shows the Virgin, the infant John the Baptist, an angel and the Christ Child in a rocky grotto, with glimpses of water and blue mountains beyond. The National Gallery points out that the cool blue-green of the distant landscape contrasts directly with the rich, warm red-brown of the earth around the figures.1 Warm near, cool far: you will meet the idea again as aerial perspective in lesson 5.

Colours shift with light, too. In Joseph Wright of Derby's Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump, which you will study in the next lesson, the lecturer's red damask robe looks salmon pink in the candlelight but darkens to magenta as your eye moves away from the flame, and the girls' dresses pass from pale lilac through purple to black.

Two cautions. First, colours in old paintings may have changed: in Velázquez's Rokeby Venus at the National Gallery, the satin sheet beneath the goddess, now grey, was originally more purple.2 Why pigments alter is a question for the sibling topic on pigments. Second, why some pairs of colours look like opposites is a fact about your eyes and brain, which the Perception topic explains with opponent channels (red against green, blue against yellow). That opposition is the subject of the next concept.

concepts.title: Complementaries: Colours at War
concepts.contentHtml:
Hues opposite each other on the painter's colour wheel are called complementaries: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet. Placed side by side, each makes the other look stronger. The man who turned this into a law was a chemist, not a painter.

In 1824 Michel-Eugène Chevreul was appointed director of dyeing at the Gobelins tapestry manufactory in Paris. The weavers complained to him that the black wools used for shading blue and violet draperies looked weak.1 As a chemist, Chevreul tested the blacks against wools dyed in the best workshops of London and Vienna and found nothing wrong with them. The weakness was in the eye: the blacks looked feeble because of the colours placed next to them. That insight led to his law of simultaneous contrast, published in 1839: when the eye sees two neighbouring colours at the same time, they look as different as possible, in hue and in strength. Grey looks faintly greenish beside red; red looks redder beside green.

Painters seized on the idea, and Vincent van Gogh pushed it to an extreme in The Night Café (1888, oil on canvas, Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven), a café in Arles at night under hazy gas lamps, with drinkers slumped at the tables. In September 1888 he described it to his brother Theo: "I've tried to express the terrible human passions with the red and the green.2" The room is blood-red and dull yellow, with a green billiard table in the centre and four lemon-yellow lamps giving off an orange and green glow. "Everywhere it's a battle and an antithesis of the most different greens and reds."

Notice what he is claiming. He calls it colour that is not "locally true" from a realist point of view, but colour suggesting an emotion. Complementary contrast here is not decoration; it is the subject. When you find two complementaries jammed together in a picture, ask whether the painter wants harmony or conflict.

concepts.title: Value: The Squint Test
concepts.contentHtml:
Of the three properties, value does the heaviest lifting. Your brain handles colour and brightness partly in separate systems, and the Harvard neurobiologist Margaret Livingstone has shown how painters exploit the split. The part of vision that works out position, depth and movement is effectively colour-blind: it responds to differences in luminance (perceived brightness), not hue.

A striking example is Claude Monet's Impression, Sunrise (1872, oil on canvas, 50 by 65 cm, Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris). From a hotel window in Le Havre, Monet painted the harbour at dawn in a few hours: cranes, smokestacks and masts dissolving in a grey mist, small rowing boats in the foreground, and an orange sun with its reflection streaking the water. The sun and the rowing boats were added at the end.1 The sun looks as bright as a beacon. Yet in a black-and-white version of the painting it almost disappears, because Monet painted it at the same value as the surrounding sky.2 Your colour system sees an orange disc; your colour-blind position system sees nothing there. Livingstone argues that this is why the sun seems to throb or pulse: its position is poorly defined to the part of vision that tracks location and motion.

Piet Mondrian used a similar effect in Broadway Boogie Woogie (1942–43, oil on canvas, 50 by 50 inches, Museum of Modern Art, New York), whose yellow and grey squares are close to the luminance of the off-white ground, so they seem to jitter.

You can test value yourself. Squint at a painting until the colours fade: what remains is the value pattern, the skeleton that carries the shapes and the depth. Or photograph it in black and white on your phone. Strong pictures usually read clearly in greyscale. When one does not, as with Monet's sun, the painter may be doing something deliberate.

title: Light and Shadow
description: Chiaroscuro, sfumato and tenebrism, from Leonardo's grotto to Caravaggio and a candle behind a skull

concepts.title: Chiaroscuro and Sfumato
concepts.contentHtml:
Shading is how a flat surface pretends to be round. Light falling on a form makes a predictable sequence: a highlight where it strikes most directly, a gradual turn into shadow as the surface curves away, and a cast shadow thrown onto whatever lies beyond. Painters call this modelling. The Italian name for strong contrasts of light and dark is chiaroscuro, literally "light-dark".

The National Gallery in London names two masters of it with different aims: Leonardo da Vinci used chiaroscuro to give a vivid impression of three-dimensional figures, while Caravaggio used it for drama.1 Leonardo's own verdict, as the Gallery quotes him, was "The artist who avoids shadows, avoids the glory of art".

Go back to the Virgin of the Rocks. The figures emerge from the darkness of the grotto as if out of mist, lit by a shaft of light from the top left. Leonardo built them up over layers of black and white underpainting2 and made the transitions from light to dark extremely gradual, so that edges blur: look at the Virgin's temples and nose. This soft, smoky modelling without harsh outlines is called sfumato, from the Italian for turning to smoke. Leonardo advised painting "without lines" in his unfinished treatise on painting, and Giorgione carried the idea to Venice.

When you look at any figure painting, find the light first. Where does it come from? Is there one source or several? Are the edges of the shadows hard or soft? Is the shadowed side of a face lost in darkness, or does it keep some reflected light? The answers tell you what the painter cared about most: solid form, atmosphere or theatre.

concepts.title: Caravaggio and the Dark Room
concepts.contentHtml:
Push chiaroscuro to its limit and you get tenebrism, from the Italian tenebroso, darkened. In a tenebrist picture, faces and hands are picked out by highlights against a mostly dark setting.1 The National Gallery calls the late paintings of Caravaggio (1571–1610) and those of many of his followers tenebrist, and his theatrical lighting was hugely influential on later painters all over Europe.

Caravaggio caused a sensation with his paintings of Saint Matthew for the Contarelli Chapel in the Roman church of San Luigi dei Francesi, and in 1601 the patron Ciriaco Mattei commissioned the Supper at Emmaus you met in lesson 2. Look at its light. A strong beam from the left falls on Christ's face and on the disciple at the right, often identified as Saint Peter, who flings out his arms in a pose that recalls the crucifixion. Christ casts a shadow on the blank wall behind him, almost like a reverse halo. The innkeeper's face stays in shadow: he has not yet "seen the light", a metaphor for spiritual understanding. Even the still life works on you. The basket of fruit teeters on the table's edge, and its shadow on the white cloth is shaped like a fish, an old symbol of Christ.

Here is a surprise about how he worked. Not a single drawing that can be firmly attributed to Caravaggio survives.2 He painted straight onto the canvas, often from live models, and sometimes scratched lines into the soft priming to mark where figures should go. Technical examination of the Supper at Emmaus found traces of drawing with a brush in dark brown paint near the wine glass, and only one significant change: the right-hand disciple's knee was moved behind the carpet to strengthen the thrust of his arm. For all its seeming spontaneity, this was a carefully planned picture by a man whose own life was anything but planned; his arrests in Rome included one for throwing a plate of artichokes at a waiter.

concepts.title: A Candle Behind a Skull
concepts.contentHtml:
Some painters hide the light source, which makes the light itself feel like a revelation. The most dramatic British example is Joseph Wright of Derby's An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump (exhibited 1768, oil on canvas, 183 by 244 cm, National Gallery, London).

It is night in a grand private house, and the moon gleams behind a cloud through the window. A travelling lecturer has put a rare white cockatoo in a glass vessel and is pumping out the air. With one hand on the valve, he looks straight out at you, as though the decision to kill or revive the bird were yours. Around the table, a gentleman times the experiment on his pocket watch, a little girl watches the bird in fascination while her elder sister covers her eyes, a young couple have eyes only for each other, and an elderly man contemplates a skull, lost in thought.

The only light is a single candle on the table, and you cannot see it. It burns behind a large glass bowl of murky liquid containing a diseased human skull.1 The candlelight is diffused through the liquid onto the faces, deepening every furrow of the lecturer's brow. Where the light does not reach, beneath the table, colour and form vanish into blackness. The National Gallery notes that Wright's strong directional light and deep shadow for drama was new in British art,2 and that he worked up to this picture through a series of candlelight scenes in the 1760s.

The light carries the meaning too. The skull and the candle are old emblems of mortality, so this scene of modern science is also a vanitas, a reminder of the passing of time, the limits of human knowledge and the frailty of life (you will read vanitas pictures properly in lesson 6). Wright leaves the bird's fate unresolved. Light and dark, like life and death, are the real subject.

title: Perspective: A Window in a Wall
description: Brunelleschi's peephole, Alberti's rules, Masaccio's Trinity and the blue haze of distance

concepts.title: Brunelleschi's Peephole
concepts.contentHtml:
Before the fifteenth century, painters showed depth by rule of thumb: receding lines usually converged, but not to a single point and not on a horizon. Then, some time between about 1410 and 1420 in Florence, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi staged one of the great demonstrations in the history of art.

Imagine standing in the west door of the unfinished cathedral, facing the octagonal Baptistery across the square. Brunelleschi holds up a small panel on which he has painted the Baptistery, its back towards you. According to his biographer Antonio Manetti, he had made a hole in it as small as a lentil on the painted side,1 opening out on the back "like a woman's straw hat". You put your eye to the hole. A mirror held in front of the panel reflects the painting back to you, so you see the painted Baptistery. Then the mirror is whisked away, and through the same hole you see the real Baptistery from exactly the same point. The two match.

The trick worked because the peephole fixed your eye at the single viewpoint the painting was built for. That is the core of linear perspective: a mathematical system in which all receding parallel lines appear to converge on one vanishing point, the point in the picture that seems farthest from you, while objects shrink in proportion to their distance.

Brunelleschi left no written account of his method, so it probably passed by word of mouth to Masaccio, Masolino and Donatello.2 Donatello's bronze Feast of Herod (about 1425), made for the font of Siena cathedral, is widely recognised as the first relief sculpture to use linear perspective. Perspective, in other words, began as an architect's experiment and spread through a circle of artists before anyone wrote it down.

concepts.title: Alberti's Window and Masaccio's Trinity
concepts.contentHtml:
Brunelleschi demonstrated; Leon Battista Alberti explained. In his treatise on painting (De pictura, 1435), he became the first to put the theory of perspective into writing.1 He asked painters to think of the picture as a window, or a thin veil (velo), through which the scene is seen: trace what appears on it and you have a correct image. He also gave a recipe, now called the costruzione legittima, for drawing a tiled floor in depth:

  • divide the bottom edge of the picture into units of one braccio, a Florentine measure of about a third of a person's height;
  • set the horizon at the height of a person standing at the front of the picture, and mark the vanishing point on it;
  • join each division to the vanishing point to get the receding lines, called orthogonals;
  • space the cross-lines by projecting them from a side view of the eye, and check them with a diagonal.

The oldest surviving perspective painting is usually taken to be Masaccio's Trinity, a fresco made around 1427 for the church of Santa Maria Novella in Florence. A pyramid of figures rises inside a painted chapel: God the Father at the top holding the cross, the dove of the Holy Spirit, the crucified Christ, the Virgin on the left looking out at you and Saint John on the right. Masaccio tooled a grid into the surface and applied perspective so rigorously that even the nails are foreshortened. He is said to have consulted Brunelleschi.

The cleverest decision is where he put the vanishing point: low down, at the mound of Golgotha, at the eye level of an average person standing in the church.2 Stand there and the painted chapel seems to open into the wall in front of you, with the holy figures above your head. Find the vanishing point in any Renaissance painting and you have found where the painter wanted you to stand.

concepts.title: Blue Distance: Aerial Perspective
concepts.contentHtml:
Lines are only half of depth. Look at a real range of hills: the far ones are paler, bluer and softer-edged than the near ones, because there is more air, haze and moisture between you and them. The painter's version is aerial perspective (or atmospheric perspective): gradual changes of colour and tone from foreground to background that imitate the effect of the atmosphere.

Leonardo studied it more thoroughly than anyone, in his writings and his pictures. In the Virgin of the Rocks, the National Gallery explains, he realised that the same colour looks different at different distances, so green appears blue from far off.1 He painted the far mountains blue and softened their edges into haze, and you believe they are miles away.

Here is the surprise: Leonardo did not invent it. According to the National Gallery, aerial perspective first appears in early fifteenth-century Netherlandish paintings and was only later taken up by Italian painters.2 Oil paint, slow-drying and easy to blend, was best suited to the delicate gradations it needs. Alberti had noticed the effect but described it inaccurately. The same Netherlandish painters built convincing spaces empirically, by eye, without the Italian geometric system.

Keep one more idea in mind: perspective is a set of conventions, not the only correct way to show space. A single vanishing point assumes a single, motionless, one-eyed viewer, exactly the condition Brunelleschi's peephole imposed. Your two moving eyes also use other depth cues, such as overlapping, relative size, texture and shading, which the Perception topic lists. Many traditions have organised pictorial space in other ways, as the sibling topic on art beyond Europe shows. When a picture breaks the perspective rules, ask whether the painter could not follow them or chose not to.

title: Reading Symbols
description: Panofsky's three levels of meaning, saints' attributes, vanitas still lifes and Holbein's hidden skull

concepts.title: Three Levels of Meaning
concepts.contentHtml:
A picture can mean things on several levels at once. The art historian Erwin Panofsky, who emigrated from Germany to the United States in 1933, set out a famous three-step method in the introduction to Studies in Iconology (1939), developed from a paper he had given in Kiel in 1931.

  • Pre-iconographic description: what anyone can recognise from everyday experience. Thirteen men at a table; a woman leaning on a wheel; a skull on some books.
  • Iconographic analysis: identifying the conventional subject, which needs knowledge of texts and traditions.
  • Iconological interpretation: reading the picture as evidence for the outlook of, in Panofsky's words, "a nation, a period, a class, a religious or philosophical persuasion".

Panofsky's classic example: a dinner table with thirteen guests is likely to represent the Last Supper.1 Iconography, then, is the study of the imagery or content of art, as distinct from its style or technique. Panofsky stressed that in practice the three levels merge into one process, but the order is good discipline: it is lesson 1's See, Think, Wonder with historical knowledge added.

The middle level runs on a vocabulary of attributes: objects, often symbolic, that identify a figure. A saint's attribute is usually tied to the story of his or her life or death.2

  • Saint Peter holds the keys of Heaven and Hell.
  • Saint Catherine leans on the wheel to which she was bound in an attempt to kill her.
  • Mary Magdalene carries a pot of ointment, because she anointed Christ's feet.
  • Saint Peter Martyr appears with a cleaver in his head, one of the instruments of his martyrdom.

In crowded altarpieces, attributes were the labels that let worshippers tell one saint from another. Small ones work in other pictures too: in Caravaggio's Supper at Emmaus, the scallop shell pinned to a disciple's clothes marks him as a pilgrim. Learn a dozen attributes and whole rooms of a museum become readable.

concepts.title: Vanitas: Still Lifes About Death
concepts.contentHtml:
In seventeenth-century Holland, prosperous people hung paintings of skulls on their walls on purpose. These are vanitas still lifes. Vanitas is Latin for vanity, but not in the sense of admiring yourself in a mirror: it means emptiness, futility.1 The idea comes from Ecclesiastes: "Vanity of vanities, saith the preacher, all is vanity." A vanitas sets symbols of human achievement and pleasure against reminders of death, each a memento mori, Latin for "remember you must die".

Read Steenwyck's Allegory of the Vanities of Human Life with Panofsky's levels. Description: a skull tilted on two books, a shell, a Japanese sword in a lacquer sheath, a pocket watch, a recorder, a lute, a shawm, an earthenware flask and a small brass lamp trailing smoke, all caught by a diagonal shaft of sunlight. Iconography: the books stand for learning, the instruments and flask for the passing pleasures of music and wine, the rare imported sword and shell for luxury, power and trade, and the watch and the just-extinguished lamp for time running out. Even the two books, one apparently new and one well-thumbed, hint at ageing.2 Iconology: a rich trading nation, proud of its wealth, reminding itself that wealth does not last.

There is a twist. The National Gallery cautions that it is always difficult to be sure why particular objects were chosen. Still lifes were also prized as displays of skill, a chance to paint cloth, metal, glass and shell, and rare objects may have been included partly as curiosities. Symbolism and showing off are not exclusive, and a good reading holds both in mind.

The same logic shapes pictures that are not still lifes. Wright's Air Pump, with its skull and candle, is a modern vanitas, and the next concept looks at the most famous memento mori of all.

concepts.title: Worked Reading: Holbein's Ambassadors
concepts.contentHtml:
Hans Holbein the Younger's The Ambassadors (1533, oil on oak, 207 by 209.5 cm, National Gallery, London) is a full-length double portrait. On the left stands Jean de Dinteville, ambassador of the French king to England, in a pink satin shirt and a black, lynx-lined cape; on the right is his friend Georges de Selve, Bishop of Lavaur, in a long brown gown. Between them is a two-shelf stand crowded with objects, in front of a green damask curtain, on a patterned marble floor.

Start with description and work upwards. The top shelf holds instruments for the heavens: a celestial globe, a many-sided sundial and other devices for measuring time and the positions of the stars. The lower shelf is earthly: a terrestrial globe, an arithmetic book wedged open at a page on division, a lute with one broken string, a case of flutes with one missing, and a Lutheran hymn book. In 1533 Henry VIII married Anne Boleyn and was breaking with Rome, and the broken string, the missing flute and the page on division have been read as a visual essay on religious and political discord. Holbein even showed two hymns, "Come Holy Ghost" and "The Ten Commandments", on pages that do not follow each other in the real book,1 perhaps because they express Christian unity.

Then there is the smear. Across the bottom of the picture floats a pale, stretched shape that makes no sense from the front. Look up at the painting from near its bottom right corner and it snaps into a2 skull. This distortion trick is called anamorphosis, and it hides a memento mori in plain sight among symbols of learning and power. At the top left, half hidden by the curtain, hangs a small silver crucifix, perhaps a hint of the hope of salvation.

The terrestrial globe even marks Polisy, about 200 km south-east of Paris, where Dinteville had his chateau and where an inventory of 1589 records the painting in the Great Hall. Imagine passing it there: from the front, two confident young men; glancing back from the side, death.

title: Beneath the Surface, Beyond the Frame
description: A worked reading of the Arnolfini Portrait, what X-rays and infrared reveal, and how context changes meaning

concepts.title: Worked Reading: The Arnolfini Portrait
concepts.contentHtml:
Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait (1434, oil on oak, 82.2 by 60 cm, National Gallery, London) is small enough to carry and one of the most argued-over paintings in the world. A richly dressed couple stand in a room. He raises one hand, apparently in greeting; her hand rests in his other palm. There is a bed hung with red, a brass chandelier, oranges by the window, a pair of discarded overshoes, a small terrier, and on the back wall a convex mirror reflecting the room and two men coming in through a door behind us. Above the mirror is a flamboyant signature: Johannes de Eyck fuit hic. 1434, "Jan van Eyck was here. 1434".

For many years the painting was understood as a record of a marriage ceremony. Readers in that tradition, following Panofsky's idea of disguised symbolism (doctrinal messages deliberately woven into everyday objects), hunted for meaning in every detail. The National Gallery no longer accepts the marriage interpretation.1 The man is most likely Giovanni di Nicolao di Arnolfini, an Italian merchant working in Bruges, and the woman is probably his second wife, whose identity is unknown.

Myth to bust: she is not pregnant. She is holding up the bulky folds of her fashionable green gown in front of her, as ladies commonly did.2 And the objects proclaim something more worldly than a sacrament: wealth and status, chosen so as not to look like aping the aristocracy. Oranges were extremely expensive, and the bed was the costliest furniture in the house, standing in a reception room rather than a bedroom.

Look harder and the room falls apart. There is not enough space for the chandelier, no sign of a fireplace, the bed is too short and the mirror seems impossibly large. Van Eyck built a perfectly convincing reality and then bent it to his purposes. Even the famous reflection is a question, not an answer: are the men in the mirror the painter and a servant, arriving on a visit? Nobody knows.

concepts.title: What X-Rays and Infrared Reveal
concepts.contentHtml:
A painting is a stack of layers, and conservators have tools that see through them. Most paint layers are transparent to near-infrared light, while carbon-based drawing materials such as charcoal stay opaque.1 So infrared reflectography can reveal the underdrawing, the artist's preliminary outline on the prepared surface. X-radiography works the other way round: X-rays pass poorly through pigments containing heavy elements, above all lead white,2 so a buried image painted with them can show up.

Both find pentimenti (singular pentimento, from the Italian for repenting): changes the artist made while painting. The National Gallery notes that these show how a design developed, and sometimes help to attribute a painting to a particular artist.

Infrared shows that van Eyck drew the Arnolfini Portrait in stages. In the first, he sketched the figures, the main furniture and the room, but left out the terrier, the chandelier, the chair, the beads and the discarded shoes, all added late.3 Arnolfini first had a larger face, a shorter robe and a bigger hat. Under the Virgin of the Rocks, the underdrawing shows that Leonardo first tried a different design. X-rays of Steenwyck's vanitas show that the flask on the right was painted over the bust of a man in a wreath, probably a Roman emperor. Velázquez first painted the Rokeby Venus's head more in profile, with her nose visible, then changed his mind.

The most dramatic recent case is Johannes Vermeer's Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window (about 1657–59, Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Dresden). An X-ray taken in 1979 revealed a painting of a nude Cupid hidden on the bare back wall, and for decades scholars assumed Vermeer had painted it out himself. A restoration project begun in 2017 proved otherwise: the overpaint was added at least several decades after the picture was made, long after Vermeer's death.4 With it removed in 2021, a standing Cupid with bow and arrows treads on two masks, a sign of sincere love overcoming deception, and the meaning of the whole picture shifts. How such evidence is used to unmask fakes is the subject of the sibling topic on forgeries.

concepts.title: Context Changes Meaning
concepts.contentHtml:
A painting's meaning does not stop at its frame. Where it hung, who saw it, how big it was and what it was called all shape what it says, and all of these can change.

Take Rembrandt's largest and most famous canvas, the militia portrait known as The Night Watch (1642, oil on canvas, 379.5 by 453.5 cm, Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam). Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, dressed in black, tells his lieutenant to start the company marching while the guardsmen fall into formation; a young girl, the company's mascot, catches the light in the background. Rembrandt was the first to paint the figures in such a group portrait actually doing something. He made it for the new banqueting hall of the arquebusiers' civic guard, the Kloveniersdoelen, where it hung as one of seven militia portraits.

In 1715 it was moved to Amsterdam's town hall, now the Royal Palace on Dam Square. It was too big for its new place, so strips were cut from all four sides, the largest from the left.1 Those pieces have never been found. The cut changed the composition. A copy probably painted by Gerrit Lundens shows that the captain and lieutenant originally stood to the right of centre, with three more figures on a bridge at the left; cropping put the action in the middle. The Rijksmuseum's director Taco Dibbits calls the off-centre placement vital to the picture's sense of movement. In 2021 the museum used the Lundens copy, which is only about a fifth of full scale,2 and neural networks trained on Rembrandt's style to print reconstructions of the lost strips and hang them around the original.

Other settings matter just as much. The Ambassadors was made for Dinteville's chateau. Velázquez's Rokeby Venus spent the early nineteenth century in a very private room of nudes owned by the Spanish minister Manuel Godoy, and has been on public display only since it reached the National Gallery in 1906. So add one last question to See, Think, Wonder: where was this meant to be seen, by whom, and is that what I am seeing now?
